result:
There is a peculiar stillness just before dawn, when the world holds its breath and the sky bleeds from indigo to pale gold. In that narrow corridor of time, everything feels possible. The streetlights flicker out one by one, surrendering to a light that asks for nothing. I’ve always loved these in-between hours—not quite night, not yet day—because they remind me how gently the world turns. We rush through our lives measuring success in milestones, but the earth measures it in seasons, in tides, in the slow unfurling of a fern. 

Sometimes I wonder if we’ve forgotten how to listen to quiet things. The scratch of a pen on paper. The distant hum of a refrigerator. Rain tapping against glass like a patient visitor. These are not interruptions; they are the rhythm beneath the noise. I keep a small notebook by the window where I catch fragments of days before they slip away: a sparrow balancing on a rusted wire, the smell of toasted bread drifting from a neighbor’s kitchen, the way shadows stretch longer in October. None of it is extraordinary. All of it is essential.

Morning coffee cools on the sill while pigeons trace lazy circles overhead. Time does not hurry, yet it arrives exactly when it must. Breathe. Notice. Begin again.

We are made of moments we barely notice until they’re gone. But if you pause, even briefly, you’ll find the world is constantly whispering its wonders. You only have to be still enough to hear them.
